Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.

- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The first sound I gave the museum was the squeak of my father's kitchen drawer. You had to lift it a little to get past the swollen part of the frame, and the squeak came just before it gave way. On the recording you can hear the spoons shift as the drawer opens. Then you hear my father say, with genuine irritation, “Well, are you going to get one or not?” He thought I wanted a spoon. I did take one, eventually, and ate a yogurt I hadn't wanted because explaining seemed like more trouble than eating a yogurt.

The museum occupied two rooms above a shoe repair shop. Its director, Ada, had been a court stenographer and still tended to watch people's mouths when they spoke. She accepted recordings on the condition that the donor could identify the sound and had permission from anyone whose voice appeared. My father signed his form on the back of a gas bill. Under the question about public access, he wrote, “Anybody who wants to hear a drawer is welcome to come over and fix the other three.” Ada filed the bill intact. She considered the offer part of the accession.

For three years I worked there on Saturdays. My favorite job was writing the labels. A boy brought us the whir of the little fan inside his mother's artificial leg; a gardener brought hail falling into an empty wheelbarrow. The difficulty was saying enough to make a person put on the headphones without telling them what to hear. I wrote that the hail sounded like a pocketful of change being flung at a tollbooth. Ada crossed it out. “Now nobody gets to hear hail,” she said. I changed the label to the date, the street, and the size of the stones.

We had regulars. A bus driver spent his lunch breaks listening to washing machines, distinguishing brands with an accuracy that frankly upset him. Two sisters came after school to play each other recordings at random and invent terrible explanations. A steam radiator became a horse learning to type. A loose shutter was a giant trying to get comfortable in a cinema seat. Ada, usually strict about noise in the listening room, let them laugh. Once I caught her trying to imitate the typing horse downstairs while the shoemaker fitted a new heel to her boot. He guessed woodpecker with hiccups.

Our most requested recording contained almost nothing. It came from a woman named Elena who had set her phone on a windowsill during the last evening before a road opened behind her house. There was a bird at the beginning, six minutes of leaves moving, then somebody far away dropping what might have been a tray. Visitors listened all the way through. They often removed the headphones slowly, as though the room outside had acquired a different pressure. One man complained that he could hear traffic over the leaves. He was hearing the street below us through an open window.

That autumn the shoemaker retired. The landlord offered us the downstairs at a rent we couldn't possibly pay, then leased the whole building to a dentist who needed somewhere to put an X-ray machine. Ada announced the closure on a postcard. She refused to call it a farewell celebration because, she said, she had already bought biscuits for the annual meeting and didn't see why the same biscuits should suddenly signify something else. Forty people came. The bus driver brought a cake shaped like a washing machine, with a single red sock revolving behind a door of clear boiled sugar.

We had arranged for the library to take the collection. The librarian arrived with padded crates, an inventory, and her small daughter, who occupied herself by crawling under the refreshment table. Halfway through packing, the girl asked why we were putting all the noises in boxes when there were plenty still happening. From under the table she could hear things we couldn't: the papery grind of cake crumbs beneath our shoes, the soft thump of a knee against a hanging coat. We got down beside her. For a minute there were seven adults kneeling on a floor that badly needed sweeping.

My father came late, carrying the drawer. He had finally got around to planing its sides and thought we might want the original object, although the original sound was gone. Without the cabinet it looked forlorn, a shallow wooden boat built by somebody with only the vaguest idea of water. Ada turned it over. On the underside, in pencil, my mother had written a telephone number. None of us recognized it. My father read it aloud twice and suddenly remembered: a woman who used to deliver eggs on Thursdays, driving a blue van with one green door.

We used the drawer to carry the leftover cups downstairs. Outside, my father held it while I unlocked the car. A spoon slid across the bottom at precisely the pitch of the spoon in the recording, and we both looked down, surprised to find that some portion of the exhibit had escaped. He laughed. I hadn't recorded his laugh for the museum. It had never seemed to qualify; he laughed every day, sometimes at jokes so poor that preserving the evidence would have been unkind. I nearly reached for my phone. Instead I took the drawer so he could get in.

At home he put it back in the cabinet. It ran beautifully. We stood opening and closing it for the pleasure of a job well done, the spoons traveling half an inch each way. After a while he filled the kettle. I found two cups and the biscuits Ada had wrapped for us in a paper napkin. From the kitchen table I could see the pale stripe his plane had left along the wood. He put the milk between us, sat down, and asked what the girls had called that horse. This time, when he tried the sound, I guessed it on the first go.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION. This is a literary short story built around a museum of recorded sounds and a family relationship.

## Grounded reading
The voice is patient, affectionate, and dryly funny, attentive to small noises and the objects that carry them. Its pathos comes quietly: the narrator recognizes that a father’s ordinary laugh never seemed worth preserving, then chooses instead to help him into the car. The story invites the reader to listen closely without turning every sound into a symbol; its ending lets shared attention and a repaired drawer matter more than the archive.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds domestic sounds—the squeaking drawer, shifting spoons, kettle, and laughter—as keepers of memory and records of everyday life. It also emphasizes the limits of preservation: recorded sounds can outlast a museum, but listening together in the present has its own value. Humor, modest acts of care, and the passing of a community through closure give the story its warmth.

## Evidence line
> For a minute there were seven adults kneeling on a floor that badly needed sweeping.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The recurring sound-object motif, dry comic details, and understated turn from preservation toward presence make this a distinctive, coherent expression of care.
